CHAPTER XXX

VIS INERTIAE (1903)

Washington in 1900, as in 1800, took its chief interest from its distance from New York, whose movement had become planetary—beyond control—while the task of Washington was still to control it. The success of Washington in the past century promised ill for its success in the next.

Hay had reached the summit of his career and saw himself on the edge of wreck. Committed to keeping China "open," he saw China about to be shut. Yet the Kaiser, breaking down all precedent, suddenly recalled his Washington ambassador and sent a personal representative—a coup d'état that detached Germany from the Russian orbit and swung her toward the west, the movement of all others nearest mathematical certainty. The scholar was studying not on Hay's account, but on his own. If Germany could be held in an Atlantic system, a century of friction would be saved.

Russia was a problem ten times as difficult. Even a cave-dweller in La Fayette Square saw, in the spring of 1903, a survey of future order or anarchy that would exhaust the power of his telescopes. Russia's irresistible inertia must crush whatever stood in her way; when she rolled over a neighboring people, she absorbed their energies into a movement of custom and race that neither Czar nor peasant could convert into any Western equivalent. The vast force of inertia known as China was to be united with the bulk of Russia in a single mass no new force could deflect.

The Atlantic must deal, then, with a continental mass of inert motion, like a glacier moving by mechanical gravitation alone. What and where was the *vis nova* that could hold its own before this prodigious ice-cap of *vis inertiae*? What were the laws of inertia?

The dictionary said inertia was the property by which matter at rest tends to remain so, and matter in motion to move on in a straight line. Adams's mind refused to imagine itself in either condition; he decided that mind moved about something it called a motive, and so long as motives were habitual, the consequent movement might be called inertia. But minds were unequally inert. Race classified thought; class-lists classified mind; no two men thought alike, and no woman thought like a man.

Race-inertia made the chief trouble in the Russian future. But sex-inertia had never been overcome at all. Of all movements of inertia, maternity and reproduction are the most typical; whatever else stops, the woman must go on reproducing, as she did in the Siluria of *Pteraspis*. The American always ostentatiously ignored sex, and American history mentioned hardly the name of a woman; yet the task of accelerating or deflecting the American woman had interest infinitely greater than that of any race whatever.

With women, accordingly, Adams talked of little else, and caught the trick of affirming that woman was the superior. At dinner one evening the question stung him to pungent rejoinder: "The American man is a failure! You are all failures!" The men laughed a little—not much. Each made allowance for his own wife as an unusually superior woman.

Gay or serious, the question never failed to stir feeling. The cleverer the woman, the less she denied the failure; she was bitter at heart about it. She had failed to hold the family together; the family was extinct like chivalry. She had failed to hold her own in the old society of Church or State, and was left, for the most part, with no place but the theatre or streets to decorate. She might have her own way without restraint or limit, but knew not what to do with herself when free.

In America the woman had been set free—volatilized like Clerk Maxwell's perfect gas; almost brought to the point of explosion, like steam. Behind the visible swarms—Dames, Daughters, brides—lay myriads of new types: type-writers, telephone-girls, shop-clerks, factory-hands, running into millions, unknown to themselves as to historians. All these new women had been created since 1840; all were to show their meaning before 1940.

The typical American man had his hand on a lever and his eye on a curve in his road; his living depended on keeping up an average speed of forty miles an hour, tending always to sixty, eighty, or a hundred, and he could admit no emotions or distractions more than he could admit whiskey. He could not run his machine and a woman too; he must leave her, even though his wife, to find her own way—and all the world saw her trying to find it by imitating him. Tragedy had been woman's lot since Eve. The Church had known more about women than science will ever know; after its overthrow she had no refuge except such as the man created for himself. She must, like the man, marry machinery.

Faust was helpless in the tragedy of woman. The Marguerite of the future could alone decide whether she would rather be victim to a man, a church, or a machine. Inertia of race and bulk would require an immense force to overcome, but might in time be partially overcome; inertia of sex could not be overcome without extinguishing the race, yet an immense force, doubling every few years, was working irresistibly to overcome it. One gazed mute before this ocean of darkest ignorance that had already engulfed society. One was almost glad to act the part of horseshoe crab in Quincy Bay, and admit that nothing ever changed—that the woman would swim about the ocean of future time, as she had swum in the past, with the gar-fish and the shark, unable to change.

Reading Karl Pearson's *Grammar of Science* and Poincaré's *La Science et l'Hypothèse*, Adams heard beneath their equations the whisper that order was a convenience and chaos the only honest assertion science could make of the supersensual; even Euclidian geometry, Poincaré allowed, was not true but merely convenient. Science had abandoned unity, and the child of 1900 would be born into a multiverse rather than a universe.
